Int J of Sci and Math Educ (2026) 24:41 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-026-10666-y

### AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing Teaching: Measurement Instrument Development 

### and Latent Profile Analysis of Pre‑Service Teachers

**Hongde Wu**[^1]** · Yimin Ning**[^2]** · Haibin Chang**[^3]** · Min Shi**[^1]** · Weizhong Zhang**[^1][ ](http://orcid.org/0009-0000-4396-4393)

Received: 17 February 2025 / Accepted: 4 April 2026 © National Science and Technology Council, Taiwan 2026

## Abstract Mathematical problem-posing teaching is a core competency for mathematics teachers. However, the rapid development and integration of artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed its implementation paradigms, imposing higher demands on mathematics teachers’ AI-Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI- TPACK). To address this, the study developed and validated a mathematics-specific AI-TPACK scale tailored to the context of mathematical problem-posing teaching by integrating AI, TPACK, and problem-posing logic. A questionnaire survey was administered to 158 pre-service mathematics teachers in East China, with SPSS 26.0 used for reliability and validity testing and Mplus 8.3 for Latent Profile Analysis (LPA). The results showed that: (1) The newly developed scale exhibited robust reli- ability and construct validity, proving suitable for assessing pre-service mathemat- ics teachers’ AI-TPACK in mathematical problem-posing teaching; (2) Pre-service mathematics teachers’ AI-TPACK were categorized into three distinct levels (low, medium, and high), with highly significant differences across all seven dimensions and large effect sizes, and AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK) emerged as the key differentiator. These findings underscore the heterogeneity of pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK development in this specific context, providing empirical evidence for designing differentiated training strategies and optimizing AI-integrated mathemat- ics instruction for problem-posing teaching.

**Keywords** AI-TPACK · Mathematical problem-posing teaching · Pre-service teachers · Measurement instrument development · Latent profile analysis

## Introduction

Mathematical problem-posing teaching is the process where students generate or reformulate mathematical problems under teachers’ guidance (Koichu, 2020; Sil- ver, 2013; Zhang & Cai, 2021), a core competency for K-12 mathematics teachers (National Council of Teachers of Mathematics \[NCTM\], 2000) and a key path- way to fostering students’ logical reasoning, creative thinking, and in-depth math- ematical understanding (Lee, 2021). Such problems can generally be categorized into three distinct types (structured, semi-structured, and free), each imposing unique requirements on mathematics teachers: structured problems require rig- orous mathematical logic to ensure disciplinary accuracy (Silber & Cai, 2017); semi-structured problems need flexible contextual adaptation aligned with cur- riculum standards and students’ backgrounds; and free problems demand open- ended creative guidance to scaffold higher-order thinking (Ngah et  al., 2016). These requirements have undergone new changes following the integration of AI technology.

The rapid development and integration of artificial intelligence (AI), including generative tools (e.g., ChatGPT and DeepSeek), have fundamentally transformed the implementation paradigms of mathematical problem-posing teaching (Egara & Mosimege, 2024; Walkington et  al., 2025). Unlike prior tools (e.g., Power- Point, dynamic geometry software), AI-powered tools have unique capabilities for the three core mathematics problem types: they can efficiently generate logi- cally consistent structured calculation problems, design adaptive semi-structured contexts, and provide intelligent scaffolding for open-ended free problems (Egara & Mosimege, 2024; Ning et al., 2024; Walkington et al., 2025). While these capa- bilities enhance the flexibility and efficiency of such teaching, they also introduce new pedagogical challenges that demand mathematics teachers to move beyond basic technology application to AI-specific integration strategies in mathematical problem-posing teaching (Celik, 2023; Karataş & Ataç, 2025; Mishra & Koehler, 2006).

These challenges underscore a critical prerequisite: AI’s transformative poten- tial in mathematical problem-posing can only be realized when mathematics teachers can integrate AI technology, pedagogical strategies, and mathematical content, which is referred to as AI-Technological Pedagogical Content Knowl- edge (AI-TPACK) (Celik, 2023; Mishra et al., 2023). Yet existing research shows that pre-service mathematics teachers who are “digital natives” (Wilson et  al., 2022) with high willingness to use AI tools generally lack specialized training in integrating these tools with problem-posing teaching (Agyei & Voogt, [2011;](#limitations) Karataş & Ataç, 2025; Segal & Biton, 2024). More importantly, insufficient research exists on pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK for mathematical problem- posing, making it impossible to accurately assess their core competencies (e.g., verifying AI-generated structured problem logic, designing semi-structured/free problems adapted to students’ cognitive levels) (An et  al., [2025;](#limitations) Cai & Rott, 2024), hampering their identification of competency gaps and the implementa- tion of targeted training (Walkington et al., 2025). Therefore, this study aims to 

AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing… Page 3 of 21 41 

develop and validate a scale adapted to assess pre-service mathematics teachers’ AI-TPACK competencies in the context of mathematical problem-posing teach- ing, and further explore the characteristics of their proficiency in this domain. Within this framework, AI is conceptualized as an intelligent scaffold for math- ematical problem-posing teaching: its core role is not to replace teachers’ or stu- dents’ problem-posing behaviors, but to assist in expanding the possibilities of mathematical problem-posing.

## Literature Review

**AI‑TPACK Framework**

AI-TPACK integrates AI with Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) to enhance teachers’ pedagogical literacy in the intelligent era, upgrading the traditional TPACK framework (Celik, 2023; Hava & Babayiğit, 2025; Mishra & Koehler, 2006; Ning et al., 2024). This framework integrates AI while retaining the original TPACK structure, encompassing three basic elements: Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogi- cal Knowledge (PK), and AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK), and four interwo- ven composite elements: PCK, AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK), AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK), and AI-TPACK (Karataş & Ataç, 2025) (as shown in Fig. [1)](#literature-review). The definition of the seven dimensions was also an extension based on TPACK (see Table 1). Compared to traditional TPACK, AI- TPACK features two critical extensions: First, dynamic adaptability, which empha- sizes real-time interactivity with AI tools (e.g., using ChatGPT to instantly modify problem parameters to align with students’ learning progress), whereas traditional

TPACK focuses on integrating static technologies (e.g., using pre-designed Power- Point presentations for teaching) (Celik, 2023; Kadluba & Obersteiner, 2025; Ning et al., 2024); Second, moral vigilance, which addresses ethical issues arising from AI use (e.g., evaluating the fairness of AI-generated problems to mitigate algorith- mic bias and safeguard student data privacy), which is a dimension absent from tra- ditional TPACK (Hava & Babayiğit, 2025; Karataş & Ataç, 2025).

However, existing AI-TPACK research mainly extends the traditional TPACK framework, focusing on framework construction, influencing factors, and empiri- cal validation. Framework studies include a seven-dimensional model (2024), a six- dimensional scale (2025), and a five-dimensional ethical structure (2025). Empirical studies highlight key influencing factors: self-efficacy, AI attitudes, digital literacy, and AI experience (Du et al., 2025; Hava & Babayiğit, 2025; Karataş & Ataç, 2025; Xu et al., 2025).Therefore, current research on AI-TPACK lacks in-depth explora- tion in specific disciplinary contexts and requires targeted and specialized meas- urement tools, especially in the field of mathematics, which is highly logical and creative.

**Mathematical Problem‑Posing Teaching and AI**

In mathematics education, “problem-posing” refers to a dynamic process where teachers and students generate, reconstruct, and clarify problems in specific contexts (Cai & Hwang, 2020; Cai & Rott, 2024). More than discovering problems, it serves as a core pathway for active mathematical meaning construction (Lavy & Shriki, 2010), centered on learners’ context perception, mathematical relationship identi- fication, and transforming vague doubts into mathematically valuable problems (Cai & Hwang, 2020; Cai & Rott, 2024), essentially involving in-depth contextual interaction (Zhang et al., 2025). Building on this, “problem-posing teaching” as a student-centered teaching paradigm refers to a form of instruction where teachers promote students’ active participation in discovering, analyzing, and deconstructing problems through systematic guidance, ultimately achieving knowledge construc- tion and the development of higher-order thinking skills (Koichu, 2020; Zhang & Cai, 2021). It serves not only as a key vehicle for stimulating students’ interest in mathematics learning and cultivating their logical reasoning and creative thinking (Cai et al., 2013; Van Harpen & Sriraman, 2013) but also as an important pathway to enhancing teachers’ own subject understanding and teaching competence (Cai & Hwang, 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Xie & Masingila, 2017). The effective implementa- tion of this teaching paradigm hinges on creating inquiry-rich contexts to stimulate students’ problem awareness. Against this backdrop, the continuous development and in-depth application of information technology have precisely provided new possibilities for creating such contexts, while the rise of generative AI has further promoted the upgrading of this practice (Mishra & Iyer, 2015; Walkington et al., 2025).

From a constructivist perspective, information technology acts as a “cogni- tive scaffolding” for students’ mathematical problems construction (Gervasoni et al., 2021; Sing, 1999; Zhang & Cai, 2021). Dynamic geometry software (e.g., 

 41 Page 6 of 21 H. Wu et al.

Geometer’s Sketchpad and GeoGebra) provides a visual, operable exploration envi- ronment (Gökçe & Güner, 2022; Ng et al., 2020; Yohannes & Chen, 2023). Dragging graphics, adjusting parameters, and observing variable relationships allow learners to intuitively perceive mathematical law formation, naturally generating doubts and refining problems (Chang et al., 2012; Ruthven et al., 2008; Wijaya et al., 2021). These tools require understanding mathematical objects’ essential attributes (e.g., geometric invariants, function dependencies) and knowledge internalization through active operation (Kadluba & Obersteiner, 2025). However, such tools have notable limitations: First, interaction is restricted by preset programs, confining exploration to teacher-defined parameters and reducing problem generation to “rediscovering” embedded mathematical relationships (Chan & Leung, 2014; Christou et al., 2005); Second, they lack intelligent feedback, failing to evaluate students’ problems (nov- elty, rigor, cognitive value) or guide problem deepening (Celik, 2023); Third, their adaptability is insufficient, failing to simultaneously meet the generation needs of structured, semi-structured, and open-ended problems. For instance, dynamic geom- etry software is more adept at supporting the exploration of structured problems but struggles to generate semi-structured contexts suitable for students’ cognitive levels or provide the flexible exploration frameworks required for open-ended problems (Prieto-González & Gutiérrez-Araujo, 2024; Stols & Kriek, 2011).

Furthermore, generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek) have overcome the aforementioned limitations, bringing new possibilities to mathematical problem- posing teaching (Segal & Biton, 2024; Walkington et  al., 2025). Compared with non-AI tools, they inherit “context creation and operational support” advantages while adding significant dynamic adaptability and intelligent interactivity (Ruiz- Rojas et al., 2023). This “generate-evaluate-guide” closed-loop capability makes AI tools efficient “problem generation engines”, as well as students’ problem-posing “conversational partners” and teachers’ teaching “collaborators” (Son et al., 2024). Essentially, this technology reshapes teachers’ roles: From “interactive environment designers/facilitators” (building inquiry platforms, providing tools) to “AI-gener- ated content evaluators, adapters, and instructional designers” (Serin & Kepceoglu, 2025). This requires mastering core AI functions: prompt design, result screening/ optimization, verifying AI outputs’ rigor and curriculum adaptability, and integrat- ing AI-generated problems with teaching objectives and students’ cognition (Celik, 2023). This role transformation places new requirements on mathematics teachers’ professional knowledge systems and further highlights the core value of the AI- TPACK framework in mathematical problem-posing teaching (Oved & Alt, 2025). Specifically, teachers need to effectively integrate mathematical CK, PK, and AI-TK to achieve the in-depth integration of AI and problem-posing teaching rather than a simple technical overlay (Mishra & Koehler, 2006; Xu et al., 2025).

However, existing AI-TPACK measurement tools lack contextual adaptabil- ity tailored to mathematical problem-posing teaching, hampering accurate capture of teachers’ context-specific AI integration capabilities (Dogan et al., 2025; Ning et  al., 2024). Furthermore, empirical research on AI-problem-posing integration remains insufficient (Zhang & Cai, 2021), and these dual gaps hinder field advance- ment. In addition, pre-service mathematics teachers (“digital natives” with strong AI acceptance) are in a critical stage of professional development (Wilson et al., 2022). 

AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing… Page 7 of 21 41 

Focusing on them helps explore the developmental characteristics of their context- specific AI integration capabilities from the source and provides a suitable research sample. Therefore, this study focuses on pre-service mathematics teachers and aims to address two key research questions: (1) Develop and validate a context-specific scale for measuring pre-service mathematics teachers’ AI-TPACK in mathematical problem-posing; (2) Explore the hierarchical and structural differences in their AI- TPACK competencies.

## Method

### Participants

To maximize alignment with the research context, we selected 180 current pre- service mathematics teachers (fourth-year undergraduates and third-year master’s students) from the mathematics education program of the College of Teacher Edu- cation at a university in East China. All participants shared identical core courses and similar K-12 internships: undergraduates completed three years of mathemat- ics coursework (e.g., Mathematical Analysis, Algebra and Geometry), while mas- ter’s students focused on mathematics education research and instructional design. Both groups had solid mathematical foundational knowledge (relating to CK) and basic information technology application skills (relating to AI-TK), as their training emphasizes integrating mathematics teaching with educational technology. A total of 180 questionnaires were distributed and 175 were collected. After rig- orous screening, 17 invalid questionnaires from participants lacking a deep under- standing of AI and problem-posing teaching were excluded, resulting in 158 valid questionnaires with an effective recovery rate of 87.8%. Among them, there were 47 males (29.7%) and 111 females (70.3%); 80.4% held bachelor’s degrees, and 19.6% held master’s degrees.

### Intervention

#### To establish a unified cognitive baseline for all participating pre-service mathemat- ics teachers and to minimize inter-individual variability in their prior understanding of the study’s core constructs, two sequentially structured, systematically designed training sessions (3-h mathematical problem-posing teaching training + 2-h AI application training) were delivered prior to formal data collection to ensure the validity, reliability, and scientific rigor of the subsequent questionnaire data. The training details are as follows.

**Mathematical Problem‑Posing Teaching Training**

The 3-h mathematical problem-posing teaching training adopted a progressive “con- cept construction—case deconstruction—practical application” framework, aiming 

 41 Page 8 of 21 H. Wu et al.

to help participants form a unified theoretical understanding and solid instructional design competence.

First, in the concept construction phase (30 min), drawing on relevant litera- ture (Ngah et al., 2016; Silber & Cai, 2017), the core connotations and boundary characteristics of three types of mathematical problems (structured, semi-struc- tured, and free) were further clarified for all participants. A total of 10 typical cases were designed for an interactive discrimination exercise, where participants were required to independently classify the problems and elaborate on their rea- soning, and the trainer provided real-time corrections based on their responses to ensure a consistent conceptual grasp.

Second, in the case deconstruction phase (60  min), building on the prior conceptual understanding, the authentic context of “school charity bazaar” was selected, and parallel instructional design cases for the three problem types were demonstrated around the core knowledge point of “linear equation in one vari- able”. Specific examples were used to explicitly align with the overall learning objectives:

- Structured problem: “Each handmade product costs 5 yuan and is sold for 12 yuan. If the total profit after selling x products is 140 yuan, find the value of x” (Objective: To help participants understand that structured problems have clear given conditions and a unique solution, focusing on training students’ algorithm execution and equation modeling abilities).
- Semi-structured problem: “Each handmade product costs 5 yuan. Design a pric- ing plan such that the total profit after selling 20 products is no less than 100 yuan; list the satisfying equations and conduct an analysis” (Objective: To ena- ble participants to master that semi-structured problems retain a certain degree of openness, focusing on training students’ scheme design and inequality analy- sis abilities).
- Free problem: “Design a mathematical problem related to ‘linear equation in one variable’ based on the school charity bazaar scenario, and explain your design intent and pedagogical value” (Objective: To help participants realize that free problems are fully open, focusing on training students’ problem-posing and crea- tive thinking abilities).

Finally, in the practical application phase (90  min), building on the learning outcomes of the previous two phases, participants were divided into heterogene- ous groups of 4–5 members according to gender and educational background, with each group collaboratively designing a complete instructional plan integrating all three problem types. This activity aimed to translate participants’ prior conceptual understanding and case analysis skills into practical instructional design compe- tence while promoting their reflection and learning through group collaboration. After completing the designs, cross-group peer evaluation was conducted, where participants were instructed to focus on the alignment of mathematical problems with knowledge points, instructional feasibility, and the consistency between prob- lem openness and teaching objectives. This process verified participants’ mastery of designing the three problem types, ensured effective training implementation, and 

AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing… Page 9 of 21 41 

aligned with the measurement instrument’s framework, unifying the core logic of training practice and research measurement.

#### AI Application Training

The 2-h AI application training was built sequentially on the 3-h problem-posing teaching training and utilized ChatGPT as the core tool and adopted a progressive “tool foundation—type-specific demonstration and practice—competency verifica- tion” framework. Its overarching goal was to equip participants with the ability to integrate AI tools into the design and optimization of the three types of mathemati- cal problems, unifying their baseline of AI-enabled instructional practice to ensure the validity of subsequent AI-TPACK measurements.

First, in the tool foundation phase (30 min), all participants were guided to com- plete uniform registration and basic function testing of ChatGPT, eliminating oper- ational discrepancies caused by tool versions or interface differences. The trainer explicitly clarified that this training was a sequential extension of the prior problem- posing training, focusing on translating the conceptual understanding of structured, semi-structured, and free problems into AI-assisted instructional design, directly aligning with the study’s core measurement objectives for AI-TPACK. Secondly, in the type-specific demonstration and hands-on practice phase (60  min), the training was divided into three sequential modules corresponding to the three problem types, with each module following a “demonstration—prac- tice—verification” procedure, where practice and verification steps were completed promptly immediately after the trainer’s demonstration. The demonstration compo- nents are as follows:

- Structured problem: The trainer demonstrated how to design clear and specific fixed problems (e.g., “Generate a calculation problem that provides the radius of a circle and asks for its area”), explaining the logic of embedding specific constraints (e.g., radius, calculation problem) to guide the AI in generating struc- tured problems with definite conditions and unique solutions.
- Semi-structured problem: The trainer demonstrated context-based variant prob- lems (e.g., “Propose two moderately open perimeter/area problems for ‘campus garden design’ involving different knowledge points”), emphasizing balanced openness and instructional focus.
- Free problem: The trainer demonstrated how to design open-ended inquiry prob- lems (e.g., “Based on the concept of a circle, propose two real-world mathemat- ics problems that allow students to explore freely”), clarifying how to stimulate the AI to creatively generate highly open-ended problems while maintaining mathematical relevance.

Finally, in the competency verification phase (30 min), each participant was required to complete an independent competency check: they were asked to use AI to generate the three types of mathematical problems within 10 min, which were aligned with the “school charity bazaar” scenario and the core knowl- edge point of “linear equation in one variable” from the 3-h mathematical 

 41 Page 10 of 21 H. Wu et al.

problem-posing teaching training, and to revise and enhance the rigor and accu- racy of the generated problems by adjusting input prompts independently. Sub- sequently, the trainer delivered a consolidated group commentary and summary. These verification dimensions are consistent with the AI-TPACK measurement framework in mathematics education, ensuring that participants can clearly and accurately optimize and expand mathematical problem-posing teaching with the assistance of AI tools.

### Instrument

This study was grounded in the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) and adopted the pre-service teacher TPACK questionnaire (Schmidt et  al., 2009). To align it with mathematical problem-posing teaching, we adaptively revised the origi- nal items (e.g., within the CK dimension, “I believe my knowledge is sufficient to cope with teaching” was revised to “I possess sufficient mathematical knowledge to effectively design and implement problem-posing teaching activities”). Moreover, to ensure content validity and item quality, three experts (two in mathematics educa- tion, one in AI education) reviewed and optimized the instrument again. Based on the above, the final instrument consists of two sections with 32 items in total (2 for demographic information and 30 substantive items), which measure pre- service teachers’ AI-TPACK competencies in mathematical problem-posing teach- ing. To illustrate the scope and design logic of the instrument, five representative items are presented below, each corresponding to one core dimension and linked to the training interventions: (1) PCK Dimension: “I can design teaching plans for specific mathematical problem-posing tasks” assesses participants’ core competence in mathematical problem-posing teaching and aligns closely with the objectives of the 3-h mathematical problem-posing training; (2) AI-TK Dimension: “I can solve common AI tool issues in problem-posing teaching” measures participants’ basic AI tool application skills, consistent with the tool foundation phase of the 2-h AI application training; (3) AI-TCK Dimension: “I can select appropriate AI tools to generate different mathematical problems that conform to mathematical logic” evaluates participants’ ability to use AI tools to accurately generate mathemati- cally logical problems, and is highly aligned with the type-specific demonstration and practice phase of the 2-h AI application training; (4) AI-TPK Dimension: “I can use AI tools to implement differentiated teaching for mathematical problem- posing” assesses participants’ competence in conducting differentiated mathemati- cal problem-posing teaching with the assistance of AI tools, corresponding to the competency verification phase of the 2-h AI application training; (5) AI-TPACK Dimension: “I can use AI tools to analyze mathematical problems raised by students and promptly correct and provide feedback” measures participants’ comprehensive AI-TPACK application competence in mathematical problem-posing teaching, and also serves as the ultimate training objective of the two interventions). All items had five response options, “Strongly Disagree”, “Disagree”, “Neutral”, “Agree”, and “Strongly Agree”, coded as 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, respectively. Detailed item distributions across dimensions and the full content are presented in Appendix.

### Data Collection

The constructed questionnaire was officially distributed via Wenjuanxing (a widely used online survey platform in China), after pre-service mathematics teachers com- pleted their internships. Notably, pre-distribution, we explained questionnaire items via three phases: (1) Concept Clarification: Explaining AI-TPACK and its dimen- sions (Table  1) with examples (e.g., DeepSeek-generated scenario-based ques- tions for AI-TCK); (2)  Interactive Question-Answer: Addressing doubts through group communication; (3) Comprehension Test: Three simple tests to ensure basic understanding of AI-TPACK and problem-posing teaching. Only when respondents answered at least two questions correctly were they allowed to proceed with the for- mal questionnaire survey.

### Data Analysis

This study mainly adopted a two-step data analysis process using SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.3, respectively. First, we evaluated the reliability and validity of the revised questionnaire as a prerequisite for subsequent rigorous analyses. After data clean- ing (screening, coding, and excluding missing values and outliers), reliability was examined using Cronbach’s α via SPSS 26.0 to test the internal consistency of the Likert-scale instrument (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994; Zakariya, 2022). Cronbach’s α \>.70 indicated acceptable reliability for both the overall scale and its seven sub- dimensions. Content validity was verified through three experts reviews to ensure structural, item, and dimensional consistency. Construct validity was assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test, Bartlett’s test of sphericity, and Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA); KMO \>.60 and a significant Bartlett’s test (_p_ \<.05) sup- ported the suitability for factor analysis; EFA was conducted using principal com- ponent analysis with varimax rotation, and items with factor loadings \>.40 were retained (Izquierdo et al., 2014; Morley, 2009).

Second, we used Mplus 8.3 to conduct Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) for explor- ing pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK competency heterogeneity. As a person-cen- tered statistical method that classifies individuals into homogeneous latent profiles by continuous variable scores, LPA prioritizes identifying distinct groups with similar competency patterns, unlike variable-centered approaches (e.g., correlation analysis), making it ideal for our study’s goal of categorizing AI-TPACK compe- tency levels (Spurk et al., 2020). Stepwise analyses from the 1-class model were performed to select the optimal model via key fit indices: Lower Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and sample-size adjusted BIC (aBIC) indicate better model fit (Muthén & Muthén, 2000); Entropy values \>.80 (range: 0–1) denoted good classification accuracy; A significant Bootstrapped Like- lihood Ratio Test (BLRT) and Lo-Mendell-Rubin Test (LMRT) (_p_ \<.05) meant the k-class model is superior to the (k-1)-class model (Nylund et al., 2007). To verify LPA classification validity, intergroup difference analysis (one-way ANOVA and post-hoc multiple comparisons) were conducted on AI-TPACK scores across pro- files (Morin et al., 2016), following confirmation of normality (Shapiro-Wilk test, 

 41 Page 12 of 21 H. Wu et al.

_p_ \>.05) and homogeneity of variance (Levene’s test, _p_ \>.05) to meet parametric test assumptions. partial η[^2] was calculated for effect size, with values \> 0.14 representing a large effect and indicating practically meaningful intergroup differences (Cohen, 1973; Kroes & Finley, 2025).

## Results

### The Reliability and Validity of the Questionnaire

First, the results showed that the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the entire ques- tionnaire was.98, and the Cronbach’s α coefficients for the seven dimensions ranged from.89 to.94, indicating that the revised questionnaire has excellent reliability and good internal consistency. Second, the KMO value of the questionnaire was.96, and Bartlett’s test of sphericity was significant at  _p_\<.001, demonstrating robust construct validity of the revised questionnaire and supporting its suitability for subsequent exploratory factor analysis. Finally, the results of principal component analysis revealed that no item had a factor loading below.50. Overall, these results confirm that the revised questionnaire exhibits good reliability and validity, making it suitable for the research analyses.

### LPA and Intergroup Differences Comparison

Firstly, analysis began with a single-category model, incrementally increasing the number of profiles to determine the optimal number of latent classes. AIC, BIC, and aBIC decreased with more classes but never reached a minimum. BLRT and LMR tests were significant (_p_ \<.05) for C-2 and C-3 models, with entropy peaking at.99 for both. However, for the C-3 model, the AIC, BIC, and aBIC values were lower than those of the C-2 model, and the rate of decrease slowed down subsequently. Therefore, the C-3 model was selected as the optimal number of latent classes (see Table [2)](#results).

Secondly, based on the scores and internal comparisons of the seven dimen- sions in the AI-TPACK framework, we identified and named the three latent classes (ranked from lowest to highest scores): the low-level group (_n_ = 71, 44.9%, Class 1); the medium-level group (_n_ = 56, 35.4%, Class 2); and the high-level group (_n_ = 31, 19.6%, Class 3). AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing… Page 13 of 21 41 

Finally, intergroup difference analysis was conducted. Since LPA identified three classes and the scores of teachers on each dimension were continuous variables, one- way ANOVA was adopted. Prior to this, normality tests and homogeneity of vari- ance tests were conducted separately on the scores of each AI-TPACK dimension. The results showed that all _p_ \>.05, meeting the prerequisites for one-way ANOVA. Subsequently, the results of one-way ANOVA on the scores of the seven dimensions showed that all _p_ \<.05 (see Table 3), and the partial η[^2] values ranged from.58 to.81, all falling into the category of large effect (partial η[^2] \>.14). This indicates that across all dimensions, there were highly significant differences among the three classes, and they exerted strong explanatory power for the variations in teachers’ AI-TPACK competencies. Therefore, post-hoc multiple comparison analysis using Least Signifi- cant Difference (LSD) was further conducted to identify the specific pairs of classes with significant differences. The results revealed that, within each dimension, all three classes showed significant differences from each other (_p_ \<.05), and the mean scores followed the order of C3 \> C2 \> C1. This indicates high-level \> medium- level \> low-level performance across all dimensions. Notably, the largest mean dif- ference across groups was observed in the AI-TK dimension (MD = 1.62, _p_ \<.001), while the smallest was in CK (MD = 1.47, _p_ \<.001). This suggests that AI tool lit- eracy is the most critical differentiator of AI-TPACK proficiency in problem-posing teaching.

## Discussion and Conclusion

This study developed a context-specific AI-TPACK scale (tailored to mathemati- cal problem-posing teaching) for pre-service mathematics teachers, explored their AI-TPACK competency latent profiles via LPA, and validated profile validity through intergroup difference analysis. The findings address literature gaps while

**Development of AI‑TPACK Questionnaire**

The validated AI-TPACK scale fills a critical gap in existing tools, responding to Lee’s (2021) emphasis on context-specific TPACK scales for mathematical prob- lem-posing. Unlike general AI-TPACK scales (An et al., [2025)](#limitations) or discipline-agnos- tic TPACK measures (Kadluba et al., 2025), this study’s scale embeds mathematics- specific problem-posing items. For example, it revises CK dimension items to focus on the mathematical correctness of problem design and adds AI-TK items target- ing the multimodal representation of mathematical problems. These adjustments respond to the unique demands of mathematical problem-posing (Mishra & Iyer, 2015) (e.g., verifying the logical consistency of AI-generated structured problems and adapting semi-structured/free problems to students’ mathematical cognitive lev- els) (Cai & Rott, 2024). With robust psychometric properties (Cronbach’s α =.98, KMO =.96), the scale supplements literature on technology-integrated mathematics 

AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing… Page 15 of 21 41 

education and provides a targeted tool for assessing pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK competencies in problem-posing teaching. This is an unmet need highlighted by Walkington et al. (2025) in their analysis of AI in mathematics instruction.

### LPA and Intergroup Differences

The LPA results identifying three distinct latent profiles: low-level (44.9%), medium- level (35.4%), and high-level (19.6%), reveal the heterogeneity of pre-service teach- ers’ AI-TPACK development, which aligns with the dynamic and context-dependent nature of the AI-TPACK framework emphasized by Celik (2023) and Mishra and Koehler (2006). The low-level group (44.9%) was the largest cohort and exhibited deficiencies across all seven AI-TPACK dimensions, with particular weaknesses in AI-TK and integrated AI-TPACK that are critical for mathematical problem-posing. For example, they struggle to use AI tools for logically rigorous structured prob- lems generation (requiring AI-TK for prompt design) or integrating AI outputs into open-ended contexts (demanding AI-TPACK synthesis). This aligns with Agyei and Voogt ([2011)](#limitations), as the 2-h AI training insufficiently addressed mathematics-specific skills (e.g., verifying AI-generated solution accuracy).

The medium-level group (35.4%) demonstrated strengths in traditional TPACK dimensions (CK, PK, PCK), enabling them to design structured problem-posing lessons based on mathematical concepts and classroom management skills. How- ever, they lack adaptability in AI-integrated teaching for semi-structured and free problems. For instance, they can create semi-structured budget-planning tasks using fractions (leveraging CK and PCK) but fail to use AI tools to provide real-time feed- back on students’ problem modifications (AI-TPK) or generate contextually diverse semi-structured scenarios (AI-TCK). This reflected a key insight identified by Celik (2023): traditional pedagogical skills do not translate to dynamic AI integration, especially in mathematics where semi-structured/free problems require AI tools to balance mathematical rigor and creative exploration.

The small high-level group (19.6%) excelled across all dimensions, mastering AI- TPACK’s unique extensions for mathematical problem-posing: dynamic adaptability and moral vigilance. They can adjust the parameters of AI-generated geometry prob- lems based on students’ spatial reasoning performance (dynamic adaptability) and identify algorithmic bias in AI-generated word problems (e.g., cultural stereotypes in numerical contexts, which relates to moral vigilance), a factor crucial for equita- ble mathematics education. This echoed the findings of Karataş and Ataç (2025) that sustained AI experience fosters disciplinary AI competence, as these teachers effec- tively use AI to bridge mathematical content, pedagogy, and problem-posing types. In addition, one-way ANOVA and LSD post-hoc multiple comparison analy- sis validated latent profiles significance and clarified competency differentia- tion. All seven AI-TPACK dimensions showed significant inter-group differences (_p_ \< 0.05), with large effect sizes (partial η[^2] =.58—.81) (Cohen, 1973; Richardson, 2011), indicating profiles explain over half the variation in pre-service teachers’ AI-TPACK and confirming practical relevance. Notably, the largest was in AI-TK (MD = 1.62) and the smallest in CK (MD = 1.47), highlighting AI tool literacy (not 

 41 Page 16 of 21 H. Wu et al.

coursework-acquired math knowledge) as the key barrier to effective AI integra- tion. For mathematics, AI-TK includes discipline-specific skills: designing prompts for mathematically consistent structured problems (e.g., algebraic equations with unique solutions) and optimizing AI outputs for semi-structured problems (e.g., text + dynamic graphs for geometric reasoning). Walkington et al. (2025) noted AI- TPACK proficiency in mathematics depends on generative AI for discipline-specific tasks (not general tech use), so pre-service mathematics teacher training must prior- itize AI-TK for problem-posing (e.g., refining ChatGPT prompts for variant struc- tured problems, validating AI free problem logic).

Moreover, consistent C3 \> C2 \> C1 mean order across dimensions confirms AI- TPACK develops as cohesive competencies. These findings inform differentiated AI-TPACK training for mathematics teacher education (aligned with problem-pos- ing context):

- Low-level pre-service teachers: Prioritize foundational AI-TK and integration skills, including AI tool workshops (e.g., ChatGPT/DeepSeek prompt design for structured problems) and guided AI practice (e.g., AI-generated fraction vari- ants), alongside short AI-integrated math internships.
- Medium-level pre-service teachers: Prioritize targeted AI-pedagogy adaptability and AI-TCK. (1) Design AI-enhanced semi-structured tasks (e.g., AI-generated budget problems, adjusting prompts for AI-TPK); (2) Align AI problems with mathematical standards (e.g., verifying AI geometry problems meet middle school curricula). Collaborative lesson design with in-service teachers refines their AI strategies.
- High-level pre-service teachers: Prioritize advanced ethical AI and innovative AI-TPACK training, mitigating algorithmic bias, AI-based student problem- posing assessment, and developing AI-integrated curricula (e.g., AI-assisted free problems + collaboration).

### Conclusion

Guided by the core demand for AI-integrated mathematical problem-posing teach- ing, which is a key competency in K-12 mathematics education (NCTM, 2000), this study developed and validated a context-specific AI-TPACK scale for pre-service mathematics teachers. Preliminary validation confirmed the scale’s robust psycho- metric properties and addressed the gap in discipline-aligned AI-TPACK measure- ment tools. LPA identified three distinct competency levels (low, medium, and high) with large effect sizes, highlighting AI-TK as the key differentiator. This study’s unique contribution lies in linking AI-TPACK to the specific demands of struc- tured, semi-structured, and free mathematical problem-posing, offering empirically grounded guidance for AI-integrated teacher education in the intelligent era.

AI‑TPACK Competencies in Mathematical Problem‑Posing… Page 17 of 21 41 

## Limitations

First, the homogeneous sample (pre-service teachers from one East China teacher education program) ensures internal validity but may limit generalizability, and thus future research should recruit diverse participants across institutions and regions. Second, reliance on questionnaire data, despite cognitive consistency enhancement, may limit insight depth. Integrating multi-source evidence (e.g., classroom observations, teaching portfolios) could provide a holistic view of AI- integrated teaching performance. Third, our cross-sectional design captures com- petencies at a specific time point, rather than dynamic developmental changes. Longitudinal designs can track competency evolution during AI training, intern- ships or initial teaching, illuminating causal relationships between interventions and growth in mathematical problem-posing contexts.
